strengths: Proposes a timely multimodal benchmark with 3.4K recent real-world images and 60K+ human-authored questions spanning perception, understanding, and reasoning tasks.
A useful design choice is to annotate multiple task types on the same image set, which can support cross-task analysis better than benchmarks assembled from heterogeneous sources.
Covers a broad range of capabilities including counting, object detection, existence, relations, visual grounding, OCR, spatial reasoning, and scene knowledge inference.
Evaluates a reasonably broad set of recent closed-source, open-source, and reasoning-oriented MLLMs, giving a helpful snapshot of current model performance.
The benchmark appears challenging: even strong models remain below 60% on the reported reasoning tasks.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to the growing set of multimodal benchmarks; the paper’s main differentiator is unified multi-task annotation on recent social-media images, but the conceptual contribution is not especially strong.

Annotation quality control is under-specified. The paper mentions training annotators, duplicate removal, and typo/format checks, but does not report inter-annotator agreement, expert verification, adjudication protocol, error rates, or validation of reasoning answers.

Evaluation reliability is a major concern: qualitative/open-ended answers are judged by an LLM evaluator, but there is no reported human-evaluator correlation, calibration study, prompt sensitivity analysis, or audit of judge failures.

The claimed synergistic effect between perception/understanding and reasoning is weakly supported. The analysis is based on aggregate model accuracies across a small number of models, so correlations/regressions do not establish task-level causal dependence and may largely reflect overall model strength.

Reproducibility is limited: the project page appears blank in the manuscript, release details are unclear, and prompts, decoding settings, majority-vote sample counts, model versions, and evaluator prompts are not described in enough detail.

The dataset collection from social media raises unresolved licensing, redistribution, privacy, and consent questions. The paper asserts compliance and masking of sensitive content but provides no concrete audit procedure, license breakdown, or release policy.

Several task definitions and metrics are underspecified, especially for open-ended reasoning, spatial direction questions, OCR, and relation extraction. It is unclear how ambiguous cases are handled and how answer equivalence is normalized.
The benchmark may contain language/cultural and geographic biases due to the image sources and examples, but this is not analyzed beyond broad scene categories.
Presentation has noticeable clarity and polish issues, including grammar errors, vague claims, and some overclaiming about avoiding data leakage simply because images are recent.

strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem: measuring whether multimodal LLMs can progress from perception and grounding to spatial and knowledge-based reasoning on the same visual inputs.

The benchmark attempts to unify multiple task types over a shared set of contemporary, real-world images, which is a useful direction compared with benchmarks whose subtasks come from unrelated data distributions.
The evaluated model suite is reasonably broad and includes recent open-source, closed-source, and reasoning-oriented MLLMs, giving a snapshot of current model behavior.
The paper includes some dataset statistics and a cross-task analysis intended to study relationships among perception, understanding, and reasoning capabilities.
weaknesses: The main contribution is not sufficiently compelling for a top-tier venue. A 3.4K-image benchmark with 60K questions may be useful, but the paper does not establish that its task design or data construction is substantially novel relative to recent multimodal reasoning, grounding, OCR, and spatial-reasoning benchmarks.

The dataset construction lacks critical detail. The paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, validation protocol, per-task annotation reliability, answer ambiguity rates, annotator instructions, quality-control pass rates, or examples of rejected/edited annotations. The statement that complex or ambiguous images were filtered out also weakens the claim that the benchmark reflects complex real-world scenarios.

The evaluation protocol is under-specified and potentially unreliable. Prompting details, output parsing, number of samples for majority voting, temperature/settings, exact scoring prompts, and evaluator calibration are not provided. Reliance on GLM4-flash as an automatic judge without human validation is especially concerning for open-ended reasoning answers.

Several metrics and task formulations are unclear. It is not explained how free-form model outputs are converted into AP50 for object detection or Acc@0.5 for grounding across heterogeneous MLLMs, and many models are marked N/A for key tasks, making comparisons incomplete.

The fairness of model comparisons is questionable. Reasoning tasks allow multiple candidate generations and majority voting, while other tasks use direct outputs; closed-source and open-source models may have different inference settings and capabilities; and there is no reporting of confidence intervals or statistical significance.

The claimed 'synergistic effects' are not convincingly supported. The correlation and regression analysis appears to be over aggregate model scores with a very small number of models, heavily confounded by model scale and family. This does not justify causal claims that lower-level abilities support higher-level reasoning.

Data leakage and contamination concerns are only weakly addressed. The paper argues that recent social-media images reduce leakage, but models may still have seen related posts or near-duplicates, and no robust deduplication against pretraining corpora or public benchmark data is described.

Ethical and legal treatment is insufficient. The benchmark uses images from social media platforms, including potentially identifiable real-world scenes, but the paper gives only high-level statements about copyright, licensing, public availability, and blurring. There is no detailed consent, redistribution, takedown, privacy, or license analysis.

The comparison to prior benchmarks is superficial. Table 1 uses coarse checkmarks and omits important dimensions such as annotation quality, answer type, scale, multilinguality, validation method, contamination controls, and public availability, so it does not convincingly position Lens against existing work.

The writing and presentation contain many grammatical errors, typos, formatting issues, and imprecise claims, which makes the paper feel under-polished and sometimes hard to trust. Examples include inconsistent naming, malformed spacing, vague task definitions, and an apparently empty project-page field.

Overall, while the benchmark direction is reasonable, the paper has major weaknesses in novelty, rigor, reproducibility, evaluation validity, and ethical documentation. I would be concerned about acceptance in its current form.

strengths: The paper proposes a timely and useful benchmark for MLLMs, with contemporary real-world images and a clear hierarchy spanning perception, understanding, and reasoning.
A key strength is that multiple task annotations are aligned to the same image set, which enables more meaningful cross-task analysis than benchmarks assembled from heterogeneous sources.

The benchmark covers a broad range of practical tasks, including object counting/detection, visual grounding, OCR, spatial reasoning, and scene knowledge inference, with examples that reflect realistic user needs.
The evaluation includes a strong set of recent open-source, closed-source, and reasoning-oriented MLLMs, and the results show that current models remain far from saturating the benchmark.
The paper is generally well motivated and the dataset statistics, task taxonomy, and comparisons to prior benchmarks make the contribution easy to understand.
weaknesses: The dataset construction and quality-control process is under-specified: there is no inter-annotator agreement, independent validation rate, error analysis of labels, or detailed annotation protocol, which is important for a benchmark paper.

The evaluation relies on an LLM judge for qualitative/open-ended answers, but the paper does not report judge validation against humans, prompt details, calibration studies, or robustness to evaluator bias.

The claimed synergistic effects are not fully established: the correlation/regression analysis appears to use only model-level aggregate scores over a small number of models, so the evidence is suggestive rather than causal or statistically strong.

The social-media image collection raises reproducibility, licensing, privacy, and long-term availability concerns; the paper states compliance but does not provide enough detail on redistribution rights, consent, or release constraints.

Some evaluation choices need more detail for reproducibility, including exact prompts, majority-voting setup, number of samples for reasoning tasks, parsing rules, and treatment of models that do not support OD/VG.

The novelty is moderate rather than transformative: many individual task types and benchmark motivations overlap with recent MLLM benchmarks, though the aligned multi-level design is a meaningful addition.
The writing contains noticeable grammatical issues and occasional inconsistencies, which do not undermine the core idea but reduce polish for a top-tier submission.

strengths: Introduces a reasonably substantial multimodal benchmark with 3.4K contemporary real-world images and 60K+ human-authored questions spanning perception, understanding, and reasoning tasks.
The unified-image, multi-task annotation design is valuable because it can support cross-task analyses that are difficult with task-isolated benchmarks.

The evaluation covers a broad set of recent closed-source, open-source, and reasoning-oriented MLLMs, and reports useful task-level results that highlight remaining weaknesses in grounding, OCR, spatial reasoning, and scene-knowledge inference.

The paper includes several useful analyses beyond a leaderboard, including temporal splits, input-resolution effects, visual-grounding scale analysis, qualitative failure cases, and a human-validation check for the LLM judge.
SMEC is simple and training-free, and the reported gains on SKI are consistent across Qwen2.5-VL model sizes and on the full test set.
weaknesses: The central benchmark contribution is weakened by insufficiently auditable dataset details: no clear release URL is provided, split construction is unclear, annotation guidelines are only lightly described, and inter-annotator agreement/filtering statistics are not quantified.

The legal and ethical treatment of social-media images is not fully convincing. Public availability and non-commercial intent do not by themselves resolve copyright, platform terms, consent, or downstream redistribution issues, and the paper leaves contact/project-page placeholders blank.

The evaluation of open-ended reasoning relies heavily on an LLM judge. Although a human preference validation is provided, the manuscript does not report the sample size, sampling protocol, confidence intervals, or error breakdowns, making it hard to assess judge reliability for the full benchmark.

The claimed “synergistic effects” are not established causally. Correlations across a small number of evaluated models are heavily confounded by model family, size, resolution, and overall capability; the oracle-style experiment feeding other task Q&A into SKI shows only modest gains and sometimes negative effects.

SMEC appears primarily to be an iterative prompt-based self-ensemble/multi-agent scaffold. The novelty over Self-Refine, multi-agent prompting, debate, and test-time compute methods is limited, and comparisons do not adequately control for number of model calls, token budget, latency, or stronger inference-time baselines.
SMEC is evaluated mainly on SKI and only with Qwen2.5-VL variants, so its generality across models, tasks, and datasets is not convincingly demonstrated.

Some experimental protocols are underspecified or potentially unfair: reasoning tasks allow multiple sampled responses and majority voting, while perception/understanding tasks use direct outputs; API/model settings, prompts, decoding parameters, and exact evaluation scripts are not sufficiently detailed in the main paper.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially claims about reducing contamination via recent social-media images, comprehensiveness, human-like intelligence, and SMEC being a principled framework rather than a test-time prompt ensemble.

The writing and presentation contain notable polish issues, including malformed spacing, typos, inconsistent appendix references, blank project/contact fields, and occasional contradictions in examples, which reduce confidence in the care of the submission.

strengths: The benchmark targets an important problem: evaluating multimodal models across perception, understanding, and reasoning on the same visual contexts rather than isolated task datasets.
The dataset appears reasonably broad in scope, with 3.4K contemporary images, 60K+ questions, eight task types, and annotations intended to support cross-task analysis.

The paper evaluates a useful set of recent open and closed multimodal models and reports task-level results that highlight persistent weaknesses in visual grounding, OCR, spatial reasoning, and scene knowledge inference.
The appendices include some additional quality-control discussion, resolution analysis, failure cases, and a small human validation of the automatic grader.
weaknesses: The central novelty is limited. A multi-task multimodal benchmark plus a prompt-based multi-agent/self-refinement framework is incremental relative to a large body of recent benchmark and agentic prompting work.

The claimed 'synergistic effects' are not convincingly established. Much of the evidence is correlational across model scores and is heavily confounded by model scale and general capability; this does not show that lower-level skills causally facilitate higher-level reasoning.

SMEC is weak as a methodological contribution. It is essentially a self-generated role prompting / multi-agent deliberation variant, with modest gains of about 3 points, tested mainly on SKI and Qwen models, without adequate compute-normalized comparisons, stronger prompting baselines, statistical significance, or robustness to prompt choices.

The evaluation protocol is under-specified and potentially fragile. Open-ended answers are graded by an LLM, but the human validation lacks sample sizes, selection criteria, inter-annotator agreement, and detailed error analysis; the reported percentage table is not enough to establish grading reliability.

Dataset quality evidence is insufficient for a benchmark paper. The manuscript does not provide rigorous annotation guidelines, agreement statistics, adjudication procedures, label error estimates, demographic/geographic distribution, or clear dataset split/access details.

There are serious reproducibility and availability concerns. The abstract's project page/contact fields appear blank, and it is unclear whether the images, annotations, prompts, and evaluation scripts can actually be released in a form that enables independent reuse.

The data collection raises unresolved ethical and legal concerns. The benchmark relies on manually collected social-media images from platforms such as X, Instagram, Weibo, and RedNote; the paper asserts compliance but does not provide convincing evidence of redistribution rights, consent, takedown procedures beyond a vague statement, or a robust privacy audit for public individuals and location-sensitive content.
Some benchmark validation choices are circular or questionable, e.g. using Qwen2.5-VL-72B for machine-assisted annotation verification while also evaluating Qwen models on the benchmark.

The comparison with prior benchmarks is shallow and checklist-like. It does not convincingly position Lens against closely related recent multimodal reasoning, grounding, OCR, and spatial reasoning benchmarks in terms of difficulty, contamination risk, label quality, and practical usefulness.

The writing overclaims significance, using phrases such as 'towards generalizable intelligence' and 'human-aligned multimodal intelligence' without evidence commensurate with those claims. Overall, the work feels more like an assembled benchmark-and-prompting package than a technically strong contribution for a top-tier AI venue.

strengths: The paper introduces a timely and useful multimodal benchmark with 3.4K contemporary social-media images and 60K+ human-authored questions across perception, understanding, and reasoning tasks.

A key strength is that multiple task annotations are tied to the same visual instances, enabling more controlled analysis of cross-task relationships than benchmarks assembled from heterogeneous sources.

The evaluation is broad and current, covering many recent open and closed MLLMs, including reasoning-oriented models, and reporting task-level results that reveal meaningful gaps in visual grounding, OCR, spatial reasoning, and scene-level inference.

The paper includes several valuable analyses beyond a single leaderboard: task correlation analysis, context-based synergy testing, resolution sensitivity, visual grounding scale breakdowns, qualitative failure cases, and temporal splits.
The authors provide a reasonably detailed annotation and quality-control pipeline, including manual verification, privacy filtering, and a human-vs-LLM grader agreement study for the SKI task.

SMEC is a simple and practical inference-time framework, and the reported gains over direct inference, majority voting, and Self-Refine on SKI suggest that multi-perspective prompting can help complex multimodal reasoning.
weaknesses: The main benchmark contribution is strong, but the novelty of the SMEC method is more limited: it resembles multi-agent/self-refinement prompting, and the paper does not sufficiently distinguish it from prior multi-agent deliberation, debate, self-consistency, or role-based prompting methods beyond implementation details.

The causal claims about synergistic effects are somewhat overstated. Much of the evidence comes from correlations across a small set of models and from context-injection experiments with modest, mixed gains; some auxiliary tasks even reduce SKI performance when added alone.

The automatic evaluation protocol for open-ended answers is a potential weakness. Although a human agreement study is included, it appears limited to SKI and does not fully characterize sample size, inter-annotator agreement, grader prompts, or failure modes of the LLM evaluator across all reasoning tasks.

SMEC is evaluated narrowly, mainly on SKI and primarily with Qwen2.5-VL variants. The gains are modest, no statistical significance or cost/latency analysis is provided, and stronger test-time baselines such as self-consistency with matched compute, debate variants, or external zoom/OCR pipelines are not thoroughly compared.

Dataset release and reproducibility are not fully convincing in the manuscript as written: the project page is blank in the abstract, licensing/re-distribution terms for social-media images remain delicate, and it is unclear whether images, annotations, prompts, and evaluation code will be fully available in a form usable by the community.

Some task examples and definitions raise concerns about annotation ambiguity and consistency, especially for spatial reasoning and scene inference. One SRC example appears to have a mismatch between the short answer and explanation, suggesting that the annotation pipeline may still contain noisy cases.

The paper would benefit from stronger positioning against closely related benchmarks and clearer evidence that Lens measures capabilities not already captured by recent multimodal reasoning, grounding, OCR, and spatial benchmarks.

The writing is generally understandable but has polish issues, including grammatical errors, formatting problems, placeholder text, and some overly broad claims about human-aligned/generalizable intelligence that are stronger than the evidence supports.
